title: Global Trade and Development
bigQuestion: Why do countries trade, and why are some countries richer than others?

story.title: One Phone, Many Countries
story.kicker: The phone in your pocket has traveled farther than most people do in a year.
paragraphs: Luis got a new phone for his birthday. On the back, in tiny letters, it said it was designed in one country and assembled in another. Luis bought it at a store in Chicago. He wondered how many countries had touched this one small thing before it reached his hand.

His older sister looked it up. The design and software work happened in one place. The chips came from factories in other countries. Some of the glass, the battery and the metals came from still other places. The parts met in a large factory, where workers put the phone together. Then ships and planes carried it across the ocean.

Luis asked why one country did not just make the whole thing. His sister had an answer. Each place does the part it does best, at the lowest cost for what it gives up. Trading lets everyone get more than they could make alone. But trade also brings hard questions about jobs, prices and fairness.

This chapter follows goods and money across borders. You will learn why countries trade, what tariffs do, and how one currency is traded for another. You will see why some countries grow richer. You will also see how Chicago became a place where the world's trade meets.
story.think: Name one thing you own that was probably made in another country. Why might it have been made there?

lessons.title: Imports and Exports
lessons.mainIdea: An export is something sold to another country; an import is something bought from another country.
reading: An Illinois farmer grows soybeans. A buyer in another country purchases a shipload. For the United States, those soybeans are an export, a good or service sold to people in another country. Illinois is one of the top soybean-growing states, so soybeans are a big Illinois export.

Now think of a banana at a Chicago grocery. Bananas grow in warm places, so most of ours come from other countries. For the United States, that banana is an import, a good or service bought from another country. Services count too. When a tourist from abroad stays in a Chicago hotel, that is a U.S. service export.

Every import for one country is an export for another. Trade happens because people want goods they cannot make well at home, or cannot make as cheaply. The U.S. both imports and exports trillions of dollars of goods and services each year.

words.d: a good or service made in one country and sold to buyers in another country
a good or service bought from another country

look.title: Import or Export?
look.text: A Chicago company sells tractors to Brazil. A family in Peoria buys a TV made in Mexico. A visitor from Japan buys a ticket to a Cubs game.
look.prompt: For the United States, label each one an import or an export. Explain how you decided.

check.q: A company in Illinois sells corn to Japan. For the U.S., this is:
check.why: Goods sold to buyers in another country are exports.

check.q: A store in Chicago buys coffee grown in Colombia. For the U.S., the coffee is:
check.why: Goods bought from another country are imports.

check.q: A tourist from France pays for a Chicago hotel room. For the U.S., this is:
check.why: Selling a service to a foreign buyer counts as an export, even inside the U.S.

lessons.title: The Trade Balance
lessons.mainIdea: The trade balance is exports minus imports; a negative balance is a trade deficit.
reading: Picture a small country that sells $50 billion of goods to the world and buys $70 billion (example numbers). Its trade balance is exports minus imports: $50 billion - $70 billion = -$20 billion. When the balance is negative, the country has a trade deficit. When it is positive, it has a trade surplus.

The United States has run a trade deficit for many years. That means Americans buy more from other countries than they sell to them. In GDP, this shows up as net exports, the NX in C + I + G + NX. A negative NX pulls measured GDP down a little.

A common mistake is to think a trade deficit is like losing a game. It is not that simple. Buyers still got goods they wanted in return for their money, and money spent abroad often comes back as investment. Economists disagree about when a deficit is a worry. Some point to lost factory jobs. Others say it reflects strong spending and foreign investment.

words.d: the value of a country's exports minus the value of its imports
when a country imports more than it exports
when a country exports more than it imports

look.title: Example Country's Trade
look.prompt: Find the total trade balance. Is it a deficit or a surplus?

check.q: A country exports $80 billion and imports $60 billion (example numbers). What is its trade balance?
check.why: $80 - $60 = +$20 billion. Positive means a surplus.

check.q: Using the table, what is the example country's total trade balance?
In the GDP formula C + I + G + NX, what does NX stand for?
check.why: NX is net exports, the trade balance.

lessons.title: Comparative Advantage
lessons.mainIdea: Two countries both gain when each makes what it gives up the least to make, then trades.
reading: Imagine two countries, Northland and Southland. In a day, a Northland worker can make 6 shirts or 3 radios. A Southland worker can make 2 shirts or 2 radios (example numbers). Northland is better at both. Does trade still help? Yes. Look at what each gives up.

In Northland, 1 radio costs 2 shirts, because making it means giving up 2 shirts. In Southland, 1 radio costs only 1 shirt. So Southland has the lower opportunity cost for radios. For shirts, Northland gives up half a radio per shirt, while Southland gives up a whole radio. Northland has the lower cost for shirts.

A comparative advantage means making a good at a lower opportunity cost than someone else. Northland should make shirts and Southland radios. If they trade at, say, 1.5 shirts for 1 radio, both get radios or shirts more cheaply than making them at home. A common mistake is to think only the country that is better at everything should make anything.

words.d: being able to make a good at a lower opportunity cost than someone else
being able to make more of a good than someone else with the same resources
the next-best thing you give up when you make a choice

look.title: Adam Smith on Buying Instead of Making
look.text: It is the maxim of every prudent master of a family, never to attempt to make at home what it will cost him more to make than to buy.
look.cite: Adam Smith, The Wealth of Nations, Book IV, Chapter 2, 1776
look.prompt: How does a family's choice to buy shoes instead of making them match the idea of comparative advantage?

check.q: In one day, Ana can bake 10 pies or 5 cakes. What is her opportunity cost of 1 cake?
check.why: 10 pies / 5 cakes = 2 pies given up for each cake.

check.q: Country A gives up 3 apples per orange. Country B gives up 1 apple per orange. Who has the comparative advantage in oranges?
check.why: Country B gives up less (1 apple) for each orange.

check.q: Northland is better at making both shirts and radios. Can trade still help both countries?
choices: No, trade only helps the weaker country.
Yes, if each makes the good with the lower opportunity cost.
Only if both have the same money.
check.why: Gains come from comparative advantage, not absolute advantage.

lessons.title: Tariffs and Who Pays
lessons.mainIdea: A tariff is a tax on imports; much of its cost usually shows up in higher prices for buyers at home.
reading: A bike made in another country sells in the U.S. for $200 (example price). The government puts a 25% tariff on imported bikes. A tariff is a tax on imports. It is paid to the U.S. government by the company that brings the bike in. That is $50 per bike.

Who really bears that cost? The importer may raise the price toward $250. Then American buyers pay more. Some of the cost may be absorbed by the foreign maker or the store. Studies of recent U.S. tariffs found that much of the cost was passed to U.S. buyers. A common mistake is to think the foreign country simply pays the tax.

Tariffs have trade-offs. They can protect jobs at American bike makers, who now face less competition. They can raise money for the government. But buyers pay higher prices, and other countries may answer with tariffs on U.S. exports, such as Illinois soybeans. Economists debate when, if ever, the protection is worth the cost.

words.d: a tax on goods brought into a country from another country
using tariffs or other limits on imports to shield home businesses from foreign competition

look.title: A Tariff on Steel
look.text: The U.S. puts a tariff on imported steel. A steel mill in Indiana hires 100 more workers. A Chicago company that makes car parts from steel now pays more for its steel.
look.prompt: Who gains and who loses from this tariff? Name at least two of each.

check.q: An imported $40 toy has a 10% tariff (example numbers). How much is the tariff?
Who sends tariff money to the U.S. government?
choices: The company that brings the goods into the U.S.
Each store's customers directly at the register
check.why: U.S. importers pay the tariff; they often pass much of it on in higher prices.

check.q: Another country answers a U.S. tariff with a tariff on U.S. soybeans. Who is most likely hurt?
check.why: A tariff on U.S. soybeans makes them costlier abroad, so farmers sell less.

lessons.title: Exchange Rates on a Trip
lessons.mainIdea: An exchange rate is the price of one country's money in another country's money.
reading: Sofia's family visits Mexico. In Mexico, prices are in pesos, not dollars. At the bank, suppose 1 U.S. dollar trades for 20 pesos (example rate). That number is the exchange rate, the price of one currency in terms of another. Currency is simply a country's money.

Sofia sees a T-shirt for 300 pesos. How many dollars is that? Divide by the rate: 300 / 20 = $15. She changes $100 at the bank. She gets 100 x 20 = 2,000 pesos. Always ask which way the rate goes. Multiply dollars by 20 to get pesos. Divide pesos by 20 to get dollars.

Exchange rates change every day. Traders buy and sell currencies, so the price moves with supply and demand. If more people want dollars, the dollar's price rises. That is why a trip can cost more one year and less the next, even when prices in the other country stay the same.

words.d: the price of one country's money in terms of another country's money
the kind of money used in a country, like the dollar, the peso or the euro

look.title: A Trip Budget in Pesos
look.prompt: Change each cost to dollars. What does the whole list cost in dollars?

check.q: At 1 dollar = 20 pesos (example rate), how many dollars is a 500-peso meal?
At 1 dollar = 0.9 euros (example rate), how many euros do you get for $200?
What mostly makes exchange rates change from day to day?
choices: Supply and demand for each currency
A fixed law set once a year
The number of banks in a city
check.why: Currencies are traded like goods, so their prices move with supply and demand.

lessons.title: A Strong or a Weak Dollar
lessons.mainIdea: When the dollar gets stronger, imports and trips abroad get cheaper for Americans, and U.S. exports cost more for others.
reading: Say the rate moves from 1 dollar = 20 pesos to 1 dollar = 25 pesos (example rates). Each dollar now buys more pesos. The dollar has become stronger. Sofia's 300-peso T-shirt now costs 300 / 25 = $12 instead of $15. Trips and imports from Mexico got cheaper for Americans.

Now flip it. A Mexican family wants to buy a U.S. product that costs $100. At 20 pesos per dollar, that is 2,000 pesos. At 25, it is 2,500 pesos. The strong dollar made U.S. goods more expensive for them. So a strong dollar tends to help U.S. shoppers and travelers but can hurt U.S. exporters.

A weaker dollar does the opposite. U.S. exports get cheaper for other countries, so farmers and factories may sell more abroad. But imports and foreign trips cost Americans more. A common mistake is to think a strong dollar is simply good. Whether it helps depends on whether you are buying from abroad or selling to it.

words.d: when a currency becomes worth more compared with another currency
when a currency becomes worth less compared with another currency

look.title: Who Cheers?
look.text: The dollar gets much weaker against the euro. Three people read the news: an Illinois farmer who sells corn to Europe, a family planning a trip to Italy, and a store that sells German cars.
look.prompt: Who is happy about the weaker dollar and who is not? Explain for each.

check.q: The rate goes from 1 dollar = 20 pesos to 1 dollar = 25 pesos. The dollar has:
check.why: Each dollar buys more pesos, so it rose in value.

check.q: A weaker dollar most likely helps which group?
check.why: A weaker dollar makes U.S. goods cheaper for foreign buyers.

check.q: At 1 dollar = 25 pesos (example rate), how many pesos does a $100 U.S. item cost?

lessons.title: Supply Chains: One Phone
lessons.mainIdea: A supply chain is every step and place that goods pass through, from raw materials to the buyer.
reading: Follow a phone backward. Before the store, it rode in a truck. Before that, a ship or plane. Before that, a factory put it together. Before that, other factories made the chips, the screen and the battery. Before that, mines dug up metals. All these steps together make a supply chain.

Companies spread the steps across countries to lower costs and use special skills. One place may have expert chip makers. Another may have many trained assembly workers. Another may have the mines. Using each place for what it does best is comparative advantage at work. Linking the world's economies this way is called globalization.

Long supply chains have a weak spot. If one step stops, everything waits. During the COVID-19 pandemic, closed factories and crowded ports delayed many goods, and some prices rose. Since then, some companies have moved steps closer to home or found more than one supplier. That can add safety but also add cost.

words.d: all the steps, people and places that turn raw materials into a product and get it to the buyer
the growing links among the world's economies through trade, travel, money and ideas

look.title: One Broken Link
look.text: A fire shuts down the only factory that makes a small chip used in a popular car. The car maker has no other supplier.
look.prompt: Trace what happens next to the car factory, its workers, car dealers and car prices.

check.q: Which is the best example of a supply chain step?
choices: A mine digs up metal later used in a phone battery.
A student reads a phone's manual.
A family pays its phone bill.
A teacher collects phones in class.
check.why: A supply chain covers the steps that make and deliver the product.

check.q: Why do companies spread phone-making steps across many countries?
choices: Because laws require at least five countries
To use each place's skills and lower costs
check.why: Each step goes where it can be done at lower cost, an idea based on comparative advantage.

check.q: What is one risk of a long supply chain?
choices: Goods can only be sold in one country.
One stopped step can delay the whole product.
check.why: Every step depends on the one before it.

lessons.title: Why Some Countries Are Richer
lessons.mainIdea: Countries grow richer mostly by making more per worker, helped by education, health, good institutions and trade.
reading: Picture two farms. On one, a family digs by hand and grows enough to eat. On the other, a trained farmer uses a tractor, good seed and weather data, and grows food for hundreds of people. The second farm has much higher productivity: more output per worker per hour.

Productivity is the main reason some countries are richer. It grows with human capital, the skills and health of workers, and with physical capital, like tools, machines and roads. It also grows with new technology. Economists often compare countries using GDP per person, which is GDP divided by population.

Institutions matter too. Institutions are the rules of the game: fair courts, protected property, honest government and stable money. When people trust that they can keep what they earn, they build and invest. Trade helps by opening bigger markets and new ideas. No single recipe fits every country, and economists still debate which steps matter most.

words.d: the amount of goods and services made per worker or per hour of work
the skills, knowledge and health that make workers productive
a country's GDP divided by its population

look.title: GDP per Person: Two Example Countries
look.prompt: Find GDP per person for each. Which country has more GDP but less per person?

check.q: A country has GDP of $800 billion and 40 million people (example numbers). What is GDP per person?
A country spends more on schools and job training. Which part of growth does this build?
check.why: Education builds workers' skills, which is human capital.

check.q: Why do fair courts and protected property help a country grow?
choices: People invest when they trust they can keep what they build.
check.why: Good institutions give people reasons to save, invest and start businesses.

lessons.title: Chicago: Where Trade Meets
lessons.mainIdea: Chicago grew as a trade hub because railroads, waterways, farms and markets all met there.
reading: Look at a map of the Midwest. Chicago sits where the Great Lakes come close to rivers that lead to the Mississippi. In the 1800s, canals and then railroads linked the city to farms to the west and cities to the east. Grain, lumber and livestock poured in. Chicago grew fast.

In 1848, traders founded the Chicago Board of Trade. It became a place to buy and sell grain, and later contracts for grain to be delivered in the future. Farmers and buyers used it to set prices and manage risk. It is now part of CME Group, and its prices are watched around the world.

Today Chicago is still a crossroads. Many major railroads meet there, and O'Hare Airport handles large amounts of air cargo. Illinois farms send soybeans and corn abroad, and Illinois factories export machinery. When world trade rises or falls, Chicago feels it quickly.

words.d: a place where many routes meet, so goods are gathered, traded and shipped
an agreement to buy or sell something at a set price on a later date

look.title: Why Here?
look.text: In the 1850s, a farmer in Iowa wants to sell wheat to a baker in New York. A railroad runs from Iowa to Chicago, and ships and trains run from Chicago to the East.
look.prompt: Explain why the wheat would pass through Chicago and how that helped the city grow.

check.q: In what year was the Chicago Board of Trade founded?
check.why: Traders founded the Chicago Board of Trade in 1848.

check.q: What helped make Chicago a trade hub in the 1800s?
choices: A law making it the capital
Waterways and railroads linking farms to eastern cities
check.why: Transport links brought farm goods through Chicago.

check.q: A farmer agrees today to sell corn next fall at a set price. What is this?
check.why: A futures contract fixes a price now for a sale later.

lessons.title: The Economic Way of Thinking
lessons.mainIdea: Economists look at choices, costs, incentives and trade-offs to understand people, markets and nations.
reading: You started this course with wants and needs. Now you can see the whole world economy. Through it all, a few ideas kept coming back. Resources are scarce, so every choice has an opportunity cost. People respond to incentives, like prices, wages and taxes.

Trade helps both sides when each does what it gives up the least to do. Markets use prices to share information. Governments set rules, collect taxes and provide some goods. The Fed tries to keep prices steady and jobs plentiful. Each step has trade-offs, and wise choices name them.

Try it on a real question. Should your town build a new park? Ask what it costs, what else that money could do, who gains, who pays, and how people's behavior might change. That set of questions is the economic way of thinking. You can use it at the store, at work and when you vote.

words.d: something that encourages people to act in a certain way, like a reward or a cost
giving up some of one thing to get more of another

look.title: David Ricardo on Free Trade
look.text: Under a system of perfectly free commerce, each country naturally devotes its capital and labour to such employments as are most beneficial to each.
look.cite: David Ricardo, On the Principles of Political Economy and Taxation, Chapter 7, 1817
look.prompt: What does Ricardo think countries will do if trade is free? What might someone who disagrees say?

check.q: A city spends $2 million on a park instead of fixing roads. What is the opportunity cost?
choices: The road repairs it did not make
check.why: Opportunity cost is the next-best use given up, here the road repairs.

check.q: A store puts snacks on sale and sells twice as many. Which idea does this show?
check.why: A lower price is an incentive that changes behavior.

check.q: Which question best fits the economic way of thinking?
choices: What did we do last year?
What would a famous person choose?
Who gains, who pays, and what is given up?
check.why: Economic thinking weighs costs, benefits and trade-offs.

review.q: Illinois sells machinery to Canada. For the U.S., this is:
A country exports $30 billion and imports $45 billion (example numbers). Its trade balance is:
A worker in Country X can make 4 cups or 2 plates in a day. What is the opportunity cost of 1 plate?
A 20% tariff is placed on a $300 imported TV (example numbers). How much is the tariff?
At 1 dollar = 150 yen (example rate), how many dollars is a 3,000-yen meal?
The dollar gets stronger. What happens to the cost of a trip abroad for Americans?
review.why: Each dollar buys more foreign money, so trips cost fewer dollars.

review.q: Which change would most likely raise a country's productivity?
choices: Better schools and training for workers
review.why: More human capital lets each worker make more.

review.q: What does the U.S. government receive from a tariff?
review.why: A tariff is a tax on imports, paid by the importing company.
